items.title: Interplay of Microbiome, Oxidative Stress and Inflammation in Health and Disease
items.summary: This review paper examined the complex relationships between the human microbiome, oxidative stress, and inflammation in the context of both health and disease. The authors synthesized current evidence on how microbial metabolites and specific probiotic strains help maintain redox homeostasis through mechanisms such as immune system regulation, modulation of inflammatory processes, and influence over mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production and antioxidant signaling. Conversely, oxidative stress and inflammation can reciprocally alter microbial diversity and function, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that disrupts homeostasis and contributes to disease development. The review highlights that while the microbiome is highly dynamic and shaped by numerous factors, its interplay with oxidative stress and inflammation is increasingly recognized as central to both physiological regulation and pathological states.
items.citation: Lourdes Herrera-Quintana, Pablo Iturbe-Sanz, Jorge Olivares-Arancibia et al.. Interplay of Microbiome, Oxidative Stress and Inflammation in Health and Disease. Antioxidants. 2026

items.title: The Oral Microbiome and Systemic Health: Current Insights into the Mouth–Body Connection
items.summary: This narrative review examined the relationships between the oral microbiome and systemic health, exploring how disturbances in oral microbial communities may contribute to diseases beyond the mouth. The authors conducted a comprehensive literature search across multiple databases, focusing on recent systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and mechanistic studies, ultimately synthesizing a curated set of articles published between 2019 and 2025. The review found clear associations between oral dysbiosis and cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, chronic respiratory infections, and adverse pregnancy outcomes, with emerging links also identified for neurodegenerative disorders, chronic kidney disease, autoimmune diseases, and cancer. Proposed mechanisms underlying these connections include bacteraemia, systemic inflammation driven by microbial metabolites and endotoxins, immune homeostasis disruption, molecular mimicry, and modulation of host metabolic pathways. The authors conclude that while evidence for these associations is growing, most findings remain observational and causal relationships require confirmation through longitudinal and interventional research, though the oral microbiome represents a promising target for systemic disease prevention and treatment.
items.citation: Ana Glavina, Dora Martić, Mark Perko et al.. The Oral Microbiome and Systemic Health: Current Insights into the Mouth–Body Connection. Life. 2026

items.title: pH-responsive nanozymes: multifunctional platforms for biomedical catalysis toward clinical translation
items.summary: This review examines pH-responsive nanozymes, a class of smart nanomaterials whose catalytic activity can be dynamically regulated by the acidity or alkalinity of their local microenvironment. The materials covered span noble metals, metal oxides, metal sulfides, carbon-based nanozymes, and metal-organic frameworks, with engineering strategies including surface ligand modification, heterogeneous atom doping, and core-shell structure design enabling precise responses to biological microenvironments. The paper surveys how these systems have been applied across biomedical contexts such as tumor therapy, antimicrobial treatment, wound healing, and anti-inflammation, where site-specific pH conditions allow controlled catalytic activation and targeted drug delivery. The authors identify persistent challenges facing clinical translation, including in vivo stability, toxicity assessment, and precise activity regulation, and discuss the potential of integrating pH-responsive nanozymes with other nanotechnologies and therapeutic modalities to broaden their clinical utility.
items.citation: Xiaofei Zhuang, Shanshan Gao, Yueqin Tao et al.. pH-responsive nanozymes: multifunctional platforms for biomedical catalysis toward clinical translation. Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology. 2026

items.title: Fluorescence-Guided Chitosan and Eugenol-Based Carbon Dots for Comprehensive Infection Control and In Vitro Wound-Healing Applications in Dentistry
items.summary: Researchers developed and evaluated chitosan–eugenol carbon dots as a multifunctional nanomaterial platform targeting dental infection control and tissue regeneration, motivated by the clinical challenge posed by Streptococcus mutans in caries and pulp inflammation. The carbon dots were synthesized from biocompatible chitosan and eugenol, then characterized for morphology, elemental composition, and surface functionalization, while their antibacterial efficacy was assessed through minimum inhibitory and minimum bactericidal concentration assays and their safety profile was tested using fibroblast viability, morphology, and migration assays. The resulting nanoparticles were spherical and nanoscale in size, with heteroatom incorporation confirmed by elemental analysis, and they demonstrated concentration-dependent antibacterial activity against Streptococcus mutans. Biocompatibility testing showed that fibroblast cells remained viable with intact morphology and exhibited enhanced migratory behavior in the presence of the carbon dots, suggesting support for wound healing processes. The authors conclude that combining chitosan and eugenol within a carbon dot framework yields a synergistic nanoplatform with fluorescence, antimicrobial, and regenerative properties suitable for oral infection treatment and wound-healing applications in dentistry.
items.citation: N. Narayanan, Aruchamy Mohanprasanth, Natesan Thirumalaivasan. Fluorescence-Guided Chitosan and Eugenol-Based Carbon Dots for Comprehensive Infection Control and In Vitro Wound-Healing Applications in Dentistry. Dentistry Journal. 2026

items.title: Online Shadow Tomography Matching the Classical Bounds
items.summary: This paper studies Online Shadow Tomography, the quantum generalization of the classical Adaptive Data Analysis problem, in which one must estimate expectation values of an adversarially chosen sequence of observables on an unknown quantum state using as few copies of the state as possible. Prior quantum algorithms for this task were suboptimal in all relevant parameters compared to classical rates, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of the quantum problem. The authors present two new algorithms that close this gap entirely, matching the best known classical bounds on the number of required copies with improved dependence on the number of queries, the system dimension, and the estimation error. One algorithm achieves the first sub-quadratic logarithmic dependence on the number of measurements combined with polylogarithmic scaling in dimension and precision, while the other achieves a bound known to be optimal among dimension-independent results. The central technical contribution is a new framework for quantifying the disturbance caused by quantum measurements, built on a quantum analogue of the Efron–Stein decomposition.
items.citation: Sitan Chen, Ryan O'Donnell, Angelos Pelecanos et al.. Online Shadow Tomography Matching the Classical Bounds. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Emulating the nonlinear effects of modified gravity on the matter power spectrum for reconstruction
items.summary: This paper addresses the computational bottleneck of calculating nonlinear matter power spectra for modified gravity models when performing model-independent reconstruction of gravitational functions across a high-dimensional parameter space. The authors built a neural-network emulator trained on a very large sample of spectra using the CosmoPower framework, targeting the nonlinear correction ratio defined as the ratio of the nonlinear to linear modified gravity matter power spectrum. The emulator was validated through comparisons with reference calculations, an independent validation set, and Markov chain Monte Carlo analyses using synthetic data, demonstrating sub-percent to percent-level accuracy across the relevant range of scales. For standard and moderate modified gravity cases the agreement with reference predictions is well within the target accuracy threshold, while even extreme nonlinear cases retain this accuracy up to a characteristic wavenumber. Beyond enabling fast likelihood evaluations, the authors demonstrate additional applications including breaking degeneracies between models with nearly identical linear power spectra, computing theory predictions for current photometric survey likelihoods, and forecasting parameter constraints from next-generation surveys using principal component analysis.
items.citation: Lanyang Yi, Kazuya Koyama, Qi Xiong et al.. Emulating the nonlinear effects of modified gravity on the matter power spectrum for reconstruction. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Dark Photons from Perturbative Decay of a Misaligned Higgs Field
items.summary: This paper examines the production of dark photons as a dark matter candidate through the perturbative decay of a dark Higgs field that is displaced from its potential minimum via stochastic misalignment during inflation. The authors revisit this framework as a simple and predictive mechanism for generating the observed dark photon relic abundance. The scenario faces constraints from structure formation, because the produced dark photons are initially boosted rather than cold, and from inflationary isocurvature fluctuations, which limit the quartic self-coupling of the dark Higgs field to small values. The analysis identifies a viable parameter space in dark photon mass and gauge coupling, which narrows further if kinetic mixing between the dark photon and the Standard Model photon is assumed at a generic level. The authors propose that this favored region could be probed by future cosmic microwave background or Lyman-alpha observations, as well as by direct detection experiments and diffuse soft gamma-ray searches when kinetic mixing is present.
items.citation: James M. Cline, Gonzalo Herrera, Jean-Samuel Roux. Dark Photons from Perturbative Decay of a Misaligned Higgs Field. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Spectrum Estimation is Almost as Hard as Tomography
items.summary: This paper investigates how many copies of an unknown quantum state are required to estimate or test its fundamental unitarily invariant properties, specifically its spectrum, von Neumann entropy, and rank. The authors establish near-quadratic sample complexity lower bounds in the Hilbert space dimension for all three tasks, showing that the required number of copies scales nearly as the square of the dimension—essentially matching the sample complexity of full quantum state tomography and demonstrating that these seemingly simpler tasks are almost as hard. The hard instances used to prove these lower bounds are constructed from sandwiched products of Haar-random projectors, with their indistinguishability established through a moment-matching argument involving Jucys–Murphy elements of the symmetric group algebra and bounding an f-divergence via high-order tensor moments. The separation between the hard instances in terms of spectra, entropies, and ranks is then derived from concentration properties of functions of Haar-random unitaries and the non-vanishing high-order components, jointly confirming all the lower bounds. Taken together, these results reveal a fundamental and somewhat surprising hardness barrier: accurately learning even coarse spectral properties of a quantum state demands nearly as much data as learning the full state.
items.citation: Marco Fanizza, Ryan O'Donnell, Chirag Wadhwa. Spectrum Estimation is Almost as Hard as Tomography. arXiv. 2026

items.title: ExtractBench: A Benchmark for Schema-Guided Enterprise Document Extraction
items.summary: ExtractBench is a benchmark designed to evaluate schema-guided extraction from enterprise documents, where an agent must faithfully extract structured information according to a user-defined schema while providing source evidence as grounding metadata. The benchmark covers thousands of pages spanning hundreds of documents across multiple business domains and document types, with a curation pipeline that combines independent-system agreement, synthetic lists with known values, and human verification to produce reliable ground truth. Evaluation measures value accuracy, record completeness, and grounding quality at both word and page levels, alongside cost, making it the first benchmark to jointly assess all these dimensions at scale. Testing revealed that commercial vision-language models perform well on short documents but frequently truncate record lists in longer ones, whereas coding agents maintain higher accuracy at substantially greater cost. A dedicated agentic extraction system achieved top rankings across all metrics, matching the accuracy of coding agents at considerably lower expense.
items.citation: Boyang Zhang, Adrian Lyjak, Eli Stewart et al.. ExtractBench: A Benchmark for Schema-Guided Enterprise Document Extraction. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Differentially Private Nonparametric Modal Learning with Applications to Regression and Clustering
items.summary: This paper addresses the problem of estimating density modes—localized summaries of multimodal distributions—under formal differential privacy constraints, a combination that had received little prior attention. The authors propose DP-GRAMS, a method inspired by mean-shift algorithms that performs gradient ascent on a differentially private score estimator, incorporating bias-reducing higher-order kernels for Hölder-smooth densities, gradient clipping, and calibrated Gaussian noise to enforce privacy. A private initialization scheme ensures high-probability coverage of all modal basins while releasing multiple starting points under a single differential privacy guarantee through correlated noise. The paper establishes asymptotic error rates for private mode recovery and derives matching minimax lower bounds, showing the proposed estimators are nearly optimal up to logarithmic factors. Two extensions to modal regression and clustering are also introduced, with experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrating competitive privacy-utility trade-offs relative to standard baselines.
items.citation: Arkajyoti Bhattacharjee, Arnab Auddy. Differentially Private Nonparametric Modal Learning with Applications to Regression and Clustering. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Innovative epitope-based ELISA assay for detecting Group B Streptococcus carriage in pregnant women.
items.summary: The paper investigated three synthetic peptide epitopes derived from *Streptococcus agalactiae* proteins—GroEL, enolase, and EF-Tu—as components of an ELISA-based immunodiagnostic test for detecting Group B Streptococcus carriage in pregnant women. The researchers developed prototype assays using these epitopes individually and in combination to detect IgG, IgM, and IgA antibody responses in serum samples from GBS-positive and GBS-negative subjects. All three epitopes, whether used alone or mixed, significantly differentiated between infected and uninfected sera, with two epitopes from enolase and EF-Tu demonstrating the strongest individual immunoreactivity at lower peptide concentrations. Combining the epitopes in various mixtures further enhanced overall immunoreactivity and diagnostic potential. The authors propose this epitope-based approach as a promising alternative to the current gold standard of bacterial culture, which is slow and can produce ambiguous results.
items.citation: Brzychczy-Włoch M, Dobrut A, Drożdż K et al.. Innovative epitope-based ELISA assay for detecting Group B Streptococcus carriage in pregnant women.. Applied microbiology and biotechnology. 2026

items.title: Bridging the diagnostic gap: the role of culture methods in the era of syndromic panels for central nervous system infections.
items.summary: This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of a syndromic molecular panel for central nervous system infections by comparing it against conventional cerebrospinal fluid culture in a real-world clinical setting over three years. Using a large dataset of paired molecular and culture results, the researchers calculated concordance, sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values for the syndromic panel both across all pathogens and when restricted to only those bacterial targets included in the panel. The syndromic panel demonstrated high specificity and a strong negative predictive value, but its overall sensitivity was notably limited, improving substantially when the analysis was confined to its included targets. Conventional culture identified clinically relevant pathogens absent from the syndromic panel, including organisms of direct therapeutic importance, underscoring that the molecular panel cannot serve as a standalone diagnostic tool. The authors conclude that optimal management of central nervous system infections requires systematic integration of syndromic molecular testing with conventional culture, and they advocate for next-generation multiplex platforms with broader target coverage guided by real-world epidemiological data.
items.venue: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
items.citation: Sberna G, D'Arezzo S, Valli MB et al.. Bridging the diagnostic gap: the role of culture methods in the era of syndromic panels for central nervous system infections.. Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology. 2026

items.title: Performance of the LIAISON PLEX gram-positive blood culture assay for identifying bacterial pathogens and resistance genes in blood cultures.
items.summary: This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of the LIAISON PLEX Gram-Positive Blood Culture Assay, a multiplexed molecular test designed to rapidly identify gram-positive bacterial pathogens and antibiotic resistance markers directly from positive blood culture bottles. The assay was assessed across multiple sites using prospective clinical samples, pre-selected samples, and contrived specimens, alongside analytical studies examining inclusivity, cross-reactivity, interference, and compatibility with blood culture bottles from multiple manufacturers. The assay demonstrated very high overall sensitivity and specificity for identifying its bacterial targets and resistance markers, with inclusivity testing detecting nearly all tested strains and only limited cross-reactivity observed among off-panel organisms. Performance was maintained in the context of polymicrobial infections and in the presence of potential interfering substances. The authors conclude that the assay offers fast, accurate, and reliable detection of gram-positive organisms and their resistance genes from positive blood cultures, with potential to support antibiotic optimization and patient management decisions.
items.citation: Chow S-K, Stevig C, Granato P et al.. Performance of the LIAISON PLEX gram-positive blood culture assay for identifying bacterial pathogens and resistance genes in blood cultures.. Journal of clinical microbiology. 2026

items.title: Validation of an in-house developed rapid assay for Group B Streptococcus detection in pregnancy.
items.summary: This study addressed the need for faster and simpler detection of Group B Streptococcus colonization in pregnant women, a key risk factor for neonatal infections and preterm stillbirth. The researchers developed and validated an in-house rapid assay combining CRISPR/Cas12a with recombinase polymerase amplification, allowing isothermal detection with results readable visually via colloidal gold test strips or by fluorescence reader. Specificity was confirmed against other common female reproductive tract pathogens, and the limit of detection was established using gradient-diluted plasmids. Clinical validation using vaginal-rectal swabs from pregnant women showed close agreement with a commercial quantitative real-time PCR method. The authors conclude that this rapid assay, completable within one hour, offers high sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy, suggesting strong potential for clinical deployment.
items.venue: International journal of medical microbiology : IJMM
items.citation: Hu S, Xie J, Liu L et al.. Validation of an in-house developed rapid assay for Group B Streptococcus detection in pregnancy.. International journal of medical microbiology : IJMM. 2026

items.title: Utility and clinical relevance of multiplex PCR panels for diagnosis of central nervous system infections.
items.summary: This study evaluated the real-world diagnostic performance and clinical utility of multiplex polymerase chain reaction panels designed to detect pathogens causing meningitis and encephalitis directly from cerebrospinal fluid samples at a tertiary care hospital over a five-year period. Researchers retrospectively reviewed test results alongside clinical data to assess detection rates, pathogen distribution, co-detections, and whether positive results actually led to changes in diagnosis or treatment. Viral pathogens dominated the positive findings, with human herpesvirus-6, enterovirus, and herpes simplex virus type-1 being most frequently detected, while Streptococcus pneumoniae was the most common bacterial pathogen identified. Despite the panels' capacity for rapid multiplex detection, fewer than half of all positive results were associated with a clinically relevant action, repeat testing after an initial negative result offered minimal additional diagnostic yield, and some tests were ordered for conditions the panels do not cover. The authors conclude that although these panels are valuable tools for central nervous system infection diagnosis, suboptimal test utilisation and insufficient clinician familiarity with panel content limit their clinical impact, highlighting the need for clearer testing criteria and improved education.
items.venue: The Indian journal of medical research
items.citation: Gürler M, Karaoğlu Ç, Yurtcu EE et al.. Utility and clinical relevance of multiplex PCR panels for diagnosis of central nervous system infections.. The Indian journal of medical research. 2026

items.title: Recent Advances in Microfluidic Chip Technology for Laboratory Medicine: Innovations and Artificial Intelligence Integration
items.summary: This review examines recent innovations in microfluidic chip technology and their applications in laboratory medicine, with particular emphasis on the integration of artificial intelligence. The authors surveyed advances in chip design and fabrication approaches, including three-dimensional printing and modular flexible substrates, alongside developments in biosensor integration that enable real-time detection of circulating tumor cells, nucleic acids, and exosomes. They found that combining these fabrication and sensing advances substantially improves diagnostic sensitivity and clinical applicability across areas such as cancer diagnostics, infectious disease detection, point-of-care testing, and personalized medicine. A central finding is that merging microfluidics with machine learning creates "smart" diagnostic platforms capable of self-optimization, automated analysis, and clinical decision support, extending the technology's reach into emerging fields like neuroscience diagnostics and microbiome profiling. The review also identifies persistent challenges in manufacturing consistency, clinical validation, and system integration that must be addressed before next-generation microfluidic devices can be routinely adopted in clinical and public health settings.
items.citation: Hong Cai, Dongxia Wang, Yiqun Zhao et al.. Recent Advances in Microfluidic Chip Technology for Laboratory Medicine: Innovations and Artificial Intelligence Integration. Biosensors. 2026

items.title: Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.
items.summary: This paper reviews advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarker research over a five-year period, culminating in updated World Health Organization policy guidance that consolidates recommendations for detecting tuberculosis disease and drug resistance into a single framework. Key developments include the expanded use of digital chest radiography with computer-aided detection as a frontline screening tool, and the diversification of decentralised molecular diagnostics through rapid nucleic acid amplification platforms, novel specimen types such as tongue swabs, and innovations like sputum pooling. Progress in non-sputum specimen testing has improved bacteriological confirmation in children and other populations who cannot produce sputum, while targeted next-generation sequencing has been endorsed for comprehensive drug-susceptibility testing at reference laboratory level. Biomarker research has advanced across transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and other domains, with host blood transcriptomic signatures showing particular promise for prognosis and triage, yet no biomarker has met the criteria required for a reliable point-of-care test capable of distinguishing infection from disease, including subclinical tuberculosis. The paper identifies remaining performance, implementation, and equity gaps as priorities for future research and development.
items.citation: Walzl G, McHugh TD, Chakaya J et al.. Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.. The Lancet. Microbe. 2027

items.title: Trends of nucleic acid - based point-of-care diagnostics for infectious diseases.
items.summary: This review examines the landscape of nucleic acid-based point-of-care diagnostics for infectious diseases, motivated by the global need for decentralized, rapid, and accessible testing outside conventional laboratory settings. The authors systematically surveyed three core operational stages of such diagnostics: nucleic acid extraction, amplification, and detection. Extraction strategies reviewed include magnetic bead-based, paper-based, and integrated microfluidic approaches, with emphasis on simplicity and equipment-free operation. Amplification methods including PCR and several isothermal alternatives were assessed for their adaptation to portable, low-power, and rapid formats. For detection, the review covers a spectrum from colorimetric and fluorescent lateral flow assays to advanced biosensor platforms exploiting CRISPR/Cas systems and toehold switch mechanisms, which offer high sensitivity and programmable nucleic acid recognition.
items.citation: Hatem H, Mysara M, Ramadan R. Trends of nucleic acid - based point-of-care diagnostics for infectious diseases.. Journal of biological engineering. 2026

items.title: A Novel Voltammetric Point-of-Care Device for Rapid and Accurate Nucleic Acid and Viral Pathogen Detection.
items.summary: This paper developed and evaluated a novel electrochemical diagnostic platform that combines isothermal nucleic acid amplification with real-time voltammetric detection for identifying viral pathogens. Rather than relying on optical readouts, the method monitors proton release during amplification by redox probing a pH-sensitive compound, circumventing common optical interference issues associated with traditional loop-mediated isothermal amplification. The system was tested against multiple respiratory viruses including SARS-CoV-2, influenza A and B, and respiratory syncytial virus using RNA from clinical samples, achieving high concordance with the gold-standard reverse transcription quantitative PCR method. The platform also demonstrated utility in an extraction-free workflow using equine nasal swabs, correctly classifying all samples for equine herpesvirus. The authors conclude that real-time voltammetric amplification is a feasible point-of-care approach across diverse sample types, while noting that broader validation in additional matrices and prospective cohorts is still needed.
items.citation: Munita R, Lyttleton R, Danefur E et al.. A Novel Voltammetric Point-of-Care Device for Rapid and Accurate Nucleic Acid and Viral Pathogen Detection.. ACS omega. 2026

items.title: Isothermal nucleic acid amplification techniques: A comprehensive overview on their principle & applications as alternative to PCR.
items.summary: This review paper examined isothermal nucleic acid amplification methods as alternatives to conventional PCR-based diagnostics. The authors surveyed the principles, detection strategies, and applications of the most widely used techniques, including loop-mediated isothermal amplification, helicase-dependent amplification, rolling circle amplification, strand displacement amplification, nucleic acid sequence-based amplification, and recombinase polymerase amplification. Unlike PCR, these methods operate at a constant temperature and therefore do not require thermal cycling equipment, making them particularly suitable for resource-limited settings where affordable and simple diagnostics are needed. The review consolidates information on reaction mechanisms, product detection approaches, and disease diagnosis applications into a single comprehensive resource, addressing a gap left by previously fragmented literature. The authors conclude that isothermal amplification methods offer strong diagnostic potential and discuss their future prospects for expanding access to genomic testing in both research and clinical contexts.
items.citation: Amare Amdiyee A, Sisay Tessema T. Isothermal nucleic acid amplification techniques: A comprehensive overview on their principle & applications as alternative to PCR.. Practical laboratory medicine. 2026

items.title: A nested PCR-based point-of-care multiplex test for detection of bacterial pathogens in cerebrospinal fluids.
items.summary: This study developed and evaluated a multiplex one-tube nested real-time PCR assay integrated with a point-of-care testing instrument for the simultaneous detection of three bacterial pathogens commonly associated with cerebrospinal fluid infections. The researchers assessed the assay's sensitivity using recombinant plasmids, tested its specificity against common CSF-associated pathogens, and evaluated its clinical performance using both simulated and real clinical samples in comparison with conventional real-time PCR following manual nucleic acid extraction. The integrated point-of-care system achieved very low detection limits for all three target organisms in simulated CSF samples while reducing total testing time to approximately two hours compared with the four hours required by the manual extraction approach. When applied to clinical samples, the point-of-care method identified additional positive cases that conventional real-time PCR had missed, demonstrating superior sensitivity. The authors conclude that this automated, culture-free system provides a rapid and highly sensitive diagnostic workflow suitable for clinical detection of these pathogens in cerebrospinal fluid.
items.venue: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology
items.citation: Wu J, Zhao Z, Pang P et al.. A nested PCR-based point-of-care multiplex test for detection of bacterial pathogens in cerebrospinal fluids.. Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology. 2026

items.title: Improving the Precision of Etiological Diagnosis in Bacterial Infections Using Molecular Technologies: A Comparative Analysis of Platforms, AI Integration, and Point-of-Care Deployment.
items.summary: This review examined the current landscape of molecular diagnostic technologies for bacterial infections, with particular emphasis on improving the speed and accuracy of etiological diagnosis in the context of rising antimicrobial resistance. The authors compared multiple platforms, including various forms of PCR, isothermal amplification, next-generation sequencing, CRISPR-based diagnostics, and digital PCR, evaluating them across analytical parameters such as sensitivity, specificity, detection limits, turnaround time, and multiplexing capacity. The review also critically assessed how artificial intelligence and machine learning are being integrated into diagnostic workflows to support antimicrobial resistance prediction and clinical decision-making. Additionally, the translational feasibility of these technologies for point-of-care deployment was considered, accounting for clinical validation requirements and real-world operational constraints. The authors conclude that advancing culture-independent bacteriological diagnostics requires carefully balancing analytical performance with clinical interpretability, and they outline key challenges and future directions for the field.
items.citation: Cotelici AM, Bălășoiu AT, Boldeanu MV et al.. Improving the Precision of Etiological Diagnosis in Bacterial Infections Using Molecular Technologies: A Comparative Analysis of Platforms, AI Integration, and Point-of-Care Deployment.. International journal of molecular sciences. 2026

items.title: Data-Centric Foundation Models in Computational Healthcare: A Survey
items.summary: This survey examines the intersection of foundation models and computational healthcare through a data-centric lens, focusing on how the quality, quantity, and characterization of clinical data shape AI performance in medical settings. The authors review a broad range of data-centric approaches spanning the full lifecycle of foundation models, from pre-training through inference, as applied to healthcare workflows. Key challenges addressed include clinical data acquisition, annotation, patient privacy, and ethical considerations that have historically hindered healthcare AI development. The survey also discusses AI security, model assessment, and alignment with human values as critical dimensions for responsible deployment in medicine. The authors conclude with an outlook on how foundation model–based analytics may ultimately improve patient outcomes and streamline clinical workflows.
items.citation: Yunkun Zhang, Jin Gao, Zheling Tan et al.. Data-Centric Foundation Models in Computational Healthcare: A Survey. ACM Computing Surveys. 2026

items.title: Biosensing technologies for foodborne pathogen detection and healthcare: principles, emerging materials, and intelligent platforms
items.summary: This review examines the current state and future directions of biosensing technologies designed to detect high-priority foodborne pathogens, including *Escherichia coli*, *Salmonella*, and *Listeria monocytogenes*, which remain significant threats to global public health. The authors survey electrochemical, optical, and microfluidic sensing platforms, analyzing how advances in functional nanomaterials, aptamers, nanozymes, and surface engineering have improved sensor sensitivity, specificity, and performance in complex food matrices. A central theme is the integration of artificial intelligence and machine learning into these biosensing systems, enabling real-time analytics, intelligent pattern recognition, and high-throughput multiplexing that transform conventional detection tools into smart diagnostic devices. The review critically addresses persistent challenges such as matrix interference, bioreceptor instability, scalability limitations, and the absence of regulatory standardization, proposing mitigation strategies including ratiometric sensing, microfluidic pre-treatment, and explainable AI frameworks. Looking ahead, the authors advocate for self-powered biosensors, modular multi-pathogen panels, blockchain-based data integrity, and standardized validation pipelines as pathways toward deployable, regulation-ready platforms for next-generation food safety monitoring.
items.citation: Purshottam J. Assudani, Balakrishnan . P., Anny Leema A et al.. Biosensing technologies for foodborne pathogen detection and healthcare: principles, emerging materials, and intelligent platforms. Microchimica Acta. 2026

items.title: Comprehensive Review on Candidemia: Epidemiology, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Future Directions
items.summary: This review examines candidemia, a major cause of hospital-acquired bloodstream infections characterized by high mortality and significant healthcare burden. The authors comprehensively analyzed the epidemiology, species distribution, and origins of candidemia alongside the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges clinicians face. The review evaluates current diagnostic methods and their limitations, emerging detection technologies, and the role of susceptibility-guided antifungal therapy in improving outcomes and managing resistance. Therapeutic strategies covered include empiric and targeted treatment regimens, management of mixed infections, host-drug interactions, and the potential of combination therapy to address antifungal resistance, as well as novel agents under clinical investigation. Looking forward, the review highlights promising future directions including artificial intelligence-assisted diagnostics, vaccine-based prophylaxis, and synergistic treatment approaches to address the evolving complexity of candidemia management.
items.citation: Haojie Dong, Minghui Song, Jingfang Sun et al.. Comprehensive Review on Candidemia: Epidemiology, Diagnosis, Treatment, and Future Directions. iFungi. 2026

items.title: Dairy cows infected with influenza A(H5N1) reveals low infectious dose and transmission barriers
items.citation: Carolyn M. Lee, Natalie N. Tarbuck, Hannah J. Cochran et al.. Dairy cows infected with influenza A(H5N1) reveals low infectious dose and transmission barriers. Nature Communications. 2026

items.title: Electrochemical Biosensors for Cancer Diagnosis and Prognosis Using Protein Biomarkers: Current Trends, Advances, and Clinical Translation Potential
items.summary: This review examines the current state of electrochemical biosensors designed to detect protein biomarkers in blood for cancer diagnosis and prognosis. The authors critically survey general strategies for electrochemical detection of serum proteins alongside recent advances in liquid biopsy biosensors targeting cancer-related proteins, with many approaches demonstrating high analytical sensitivity. The review identifies key obstacles preventing these technologies from reaching clinical practice, including matrix effects from complex biological samples, insufficient validation with patient samples, interpatient variability, and practical manufacturing and stability challenges. Particular emphasis is placed on the analytical and clinical validation frameworks needed to make such biosensors clinically translatable and commercially viable. The work positions electrochemical liquid biopsy assays as promising but still immature tools for non-invasive cancer screening that require more rigorous standardization and real-world validation before widespread clinical adoption.
items.citation: Michael E. J. Lopez Mujica, Elena E. Ferapontova. Electrochemical Biosensors for Cancer Diagnosis and Prognosis Using Protein Biomarkers: Current Trends, Advances, and Clinical Translation Potential. Sensors. 2026

items.title: Emulating the nonlinear effects of modified gravity on the matter power spectrum for reconstruction
items.summary: This paper addresses the computational bottleneck in testing modified gravity theories against cosmological data, specifically the expensive calculation of nonlinear matter power spectra required for model-independent reconstruction of modified gravity functions. The authors built a neural-network emulator trained on a very large set of samples using the CosmoPower framework to predict the nonlinear correction factor defined as the ratio of the nonlinear to linear modified gravity matter power spectrum. The emulator achieves sub-percent to roughly one-and-a-half percent accuracy across the relevant range of scales for standard and moderately modified cosmologies, with performance maintained into the nonlinear regime for less extreme cases. Validation through independent test sets and synthetic Markov chain Monte Carlo analyses confirmed that the emulator reliably recovers standard cosmological parameters and the general relativity limits of modified gravity functions, demonstrating its suitability for Stage-IV survey analyses. The authors further illustrated the emulator's utility in three practical applications: breaking degeneracies between models with similar linear spectra, enabling likelihood evaluations for current photometric surveys, and forecasting joint constraints from upcoming spectroscopic and imaging surveys using principal component analysis.
items.citation: Lanyang Yi, Kazuya Koyama, Qi Xiong et al.. Emulating the nonlinear effects of modified gravity on the matter power spectrum for reconstruction. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Dark Photons from Perturbative Decay of a Misaligned Higgs Field
items.summary: This paper examines the production of dark photons as a dark matter candidate through the perturbative decay of a dark Higgs field that is displaced from its potential minimum during inflation, a mechanism known as stochastic misalignment. The authors analyze the constraints on this framework arising from structure formation, since the produced dark photons are initially relativistic and thus boosted, and from inflationary isocurvature fluctuations, which require the dark Higgs quartic coupling to be small. They map out a viable parameter space of dark photon masses and gauge couplings consistent with these constraints, finding that the allowed region narrows further if kinetic mixing between the dark photon and the Standard Model photon is present at a generic level. The study finds that the favored parameter space could be probed by future cosmic microwave background or Lyman-alpha observations, and, if kinetic mixing exists, by direct detection experiments or diffuse soft gamma-ray searches.
items.citation: James M. Cline, Gonzalo Herrera, Jean-Samuel Roux. Dark Photons from Perturbative Decay of a Misaligned Higgs Field. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Spectrum Estimation is Almost as Hard as Tomography
items.summary: This paper investigates how many copies of an unknown quantum state are required to estimate or test its fundamental properties, specifically focusing on spectrum estimation, von Neumann entropy estimation, and rank-testing. The authors establish sample complexity lower bounds for these tasks on quantum states in dimension d, showing that nearly quadratic in d samples are necessary even for constant-error guarantees. To prove these bounds, they construct hard-to-distinguish pairs of quantum states built from sandwiched products of Haar-random projectors, using a novel normalization technique to compute high-order tensor moments expressed as symmetric functions of Jucys–Murphy elements in the symmetric group algebra. Indistinguishability between these state pairs is demonstrated via log-likelihood ratio analysis and moment-matching, while an f-divergence bound on high-order components seals the argument. The results imply that estimating spectral properties of quantum states is nearly as hard as full quantum state tomography, which also requires on the order of d squared samples.
items.citation: Marco Fanizza, Ryan O'Donnell, Chirag Wadhwa. Spectrum Estimation is Almost as Hard as Tomography. arXiv. 2026

items.title: ArcLP: A Matlab implementation of an $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n}L)$ arc-search infeasible interior-point algorithm for linear programming
items.summary: This paper presents a Matlab software implementation of an arc-search infeasible interior-point algorithm for linear programming that carries the best known polynomial complexity bound among interior-point methods for this problem class. The implementation is described in terms of its software architecture, key algorithmic strategies, and ease of use. The software was extensively tested on standard Netlib benchmark linear programming problems, including large-scale instances with tens of thousands of constraints and hundreds of thousands of variables, and successfully found optimal solutions in all cases. Computational results were compared against the widely used Mehrotra predictor-corrector algorithm, and the arc-search method proved to be competitive in practice. The authors conclude that the algorithm achieves both the strongest theoretical complexity guarantee and practical computational performance comparable to a popular state-of-the-art method.
items.citation: Yang, Yaguang. ArcLP: A Matlab implementation of an $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n}L)$ arc-search infeasible interior-point algorithm for linear programming. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Fermionic entropy: an efficiently measurable strong monotone for non-Gaussianity
items.summary: This paper investigates fermionic non-Gaussianity as a quantum resource, focusing on how to quantify and measure the departure from fermionic Gaussian states, which are the classically simulable baseline for fermionic systems. The authors show that the fermionic entropy, defined via the squared Frobenius norm of the correlation matrix, is a strong pure-state Gaussian monotone with a simple closed-form expression. They demonstrate that the associated fermionic purity can be estimated with a constant number of two-copy measurements independent of system size, prove asymptotic continuity to establish its operational meaning as an upper bound on the non-Gaussianity distillation rate, and derive a sample complexity bound for tolerant testing of Gaussian states that improves quadratically over prior work. As a further application, they analyze Matchgate circuits supplemented with non-Gaussian local gates and prove that a linear number of such gates is necessary to approximate a state 2-design, which, combined with known upper bounds, determines the optimal non-Gaussian gate count up to logarithmic factors and quantifies the extensive non-Gaussianity cost of generating Haar-random-like quantum dynamics in this architecture.
items.citation: Lorenzo Leone, Lennart Bittel. Fermionic entropy: an efficiently measurable strong monotone for non-Gaussianity. arXiv. 2026

items.title: The IACOB project XIX. Revisiting massive-star evolution with empirical TAMS constraints: updated models, overshoot calibration, and the population of blue supergiants
items.summary: This study investigates the physical processes governing massive star evolution, with particular focus on convective boundary mixing efficiency and its role in setting the width of the main sequence. Using empirical observations of massive Galactic stars from the IACOB database, the researchers calibrated the location of the terminal-age main sequence to constrain convective overshooting, and then tested single-star evolutionary models by comparing synthetic populations against observed stellar properties. The modelling required a mass-dependent overshooting efficiency to reproduce the empirical main-sequence width, and rotational properties of observed populations were well reproduced by single-star models regardless of the angular momentum transport prescription used, a success attributed to updated wind prescriptions rather than assumptions about internal transport. However, the models could not account for the observed dependence of the terminal-age main sequence location on rotation rate. The study also finds that single-star evolution alone is insufficient to explain the population of blue supergiants lying to the right of the terminal-age main sequence, implying that binary interactions or other processes must be invoked.
items.citation: Luca Sciarini, Abel de Burgos, Sophie Rosu et al.. The IACOB project XIX. Revisiting massive-star evolution with empirical TAMS constraints: updated models, overshoot calibration, and the population of blue supergiants. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Evaluation of the QuickFinder COVID-19/Flu/RSV antigen test for rapid simultaneous detection of SARS-CoV-2, influenza A/B viruses, and respiratory syncytial virus.
items.summary: This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of a lateral flow immunoassay-based antigen rapid diagnostic test designed to simultaneously detect SARS-CoV-2, influenza A and B viruses, and respiratory syncytial virus from nasopharyngeal swab specimens. The test was compared against real-time reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction as a reference standard using archived clinical specimens, and cross-reactivity was assessed against a panel of respiratory viral and bacterial pathogens. The test demonstrated high sensitivity for influenza A and SARS-CoV-2, somewhat lower sensitivity for influenza B and RSV, and complete specificity for all four targets with no cross-reactivity observed. Sensitivity was consistently high in specimens with high viral loads but declined in low viral load specimens, reflecting a known limitation of antigen-based detection approaches. The authors conclude that while the test is a reliable rapid screening tool for initial differentiation of major respiratory viruses, it should complement rather than replace molecular testing.
items.citation: Kim JA, Kang M, Yu HJ et al.. Evaluation of the QuickFinder COVID-19/Flu/RSV antigen test for rapid simultaneous detection of SARS-CoV-2, influenza A/B viruses, and respiratory syncytial virus.. Diagnostic microbiology and infectious disease. 2026

items.title: No detection of respiratory syncytial virus at one clinic in Japan with rapid immunochromatographic antigen tests for three viruses using the same nasopharyngeal swabs from adult patients
items.summary: This study investigated the disease burden of respiratory syncytial virus in adult patients at a Japanese clinic by testing nasopharyngeal swabs collected from patients presenting with acute respiratory infection symptoms. Rapid immunochromatographic antigen tests were used to simultaneously screen for SARS-CoV-2, influenza A and B viruses, and RSV. While the tests detected positive cases for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza viruses, no RSV-positive patients were identified. Comparing these findings against previous reports using PCR testing, which identified substantially more RSV-positive cases, revealed a statistically significant difference in detection rates. The authors conclude that rapid immunochromatographic antigen testing has limited usefulness for diagnosing RSV infections in Japanese adults compared to PCR-based approaches.
items.citation: Kajiwara N, Tsunetoshi Y, Shiode S. No detection of respiratory syncytial virus at one clinic in Japan with rapid immunochromatographic antigen tests for three viruses using the same nasopharyngeal swabs from adult patients. 2026

items.title: Performance of an antigen test for detection of SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus-a prospective study.
items.summary: This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of a multiplex rapid antigen test capable of simultaneously detecting SARS-CoV-2, influenza A, influenza B, and respiratory syncytial virus in patients presenting with acute respiratory infection symptoms. A prospective design was used in which symptomatic patients, including a subset of children, underwent both the nasal swab rapid antigen test administered by emergency department staff and a separately collected nasopharyngeal PCR test at a central laboratory. The test demonstrated high sensitivity for all four pathogens when PCR cycle threshold values indicated higher viral loads, and achieved perfect specificity across all agents and age groups. An additional analysis revealed that nasal swabs absorbed less viral RNA than nasopharyngeal swabs, a difference that was statistically significant for influenza A among the full patient cohort but not observed in children. The authors conclude that the test's performance profile supports its potential use as a marker of infectiousness in acute clinical care settings.
items.venue: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
items.citation: Berger K, Vang SH, Bekkeseth RHO et al.. Performance of an antigen test for detection of SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus-a prospective study.. Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases. 2026

items.title: Respiratory surveillance through point of care molecular testing and its impacts on nursing home RSV, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2 awareness and reporting behavior: a pilot study.
items.citation: Davidson H, Han L, McConeghy K et al.. Respiratory surveillance through point of care molecular testing and its impacts on nursing home RSV, influenza, and SARS-CoV-2 awareness and reporting behavior: a pilot study.. Antimicrobial stewardship & healthcare epidemiology : ASHE. 2026

items.title: Analytical comparison of over-the-counter multiplex tests for influenza A, influenza B, and SARS-CoV-2.
items.summary: This study evaluated the analytical performance of over-the-counter lateral flow tests designed to detect influenza A, influenza B, and SARS-CoV-2 in a controlled, head-to-head comparison. Researchers prepared contrived specimen panels from propagated viral stocks of multiple influenza strains and a SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant in clinical matrix, then applied these to eight commercially available tests purchased from United States retailers, following each manufacturer's instructions with blinded result interpretation. Detection limits were broadly similar across all eight tests and all four viruses, falling within a fourfold dilution range of one another. A key finding was that at low viral concentrations, many tests initially read as negative at the beginning of the stated interpretation window but converted to a positive result by the end of that window. The authors therefore recommend that users allow the full manufacturer-specified incubation time to elapse before concluding a test result is truly negative.
items.citation: Lohsen S, Hoy-Schulz Y, Taing A et al.. Analytical comparison of over-the-counter multiplex tests for influenza A, influenza B, and SARS-CoV-2.. Microbiology spectrum. 2026

items.title: No detection of respiratory syncytial virus at one clinic in Japan with rapid immunochromatographic antigen tests for three viruses using the same nasopharyngeal swabs from adult patients
items.summary: The study investigated the disease burden of respiratory syncytial virus in Japanese adults by testing nasopharyngeal swabs from adult patients presenting with acute respiratory infection symptoms at a clinic over approximately one year. Rapid immunochromatographic antigen tests detecting SARS-CoV-2, influenza A and B, and RSV were applied to all collected samples. While substantial numbers of patients tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A, and one tested positive for influenza B, no patients tested positive for RSV. Comparing these findings against previous reports that used polymerase chain reaction testing revealed a statistically significant difference in RSV detection rates. The authors conclude that rapid immunochromatographic antigen testing is not a useful diagnostic approach for RSV infection in adult patients in Japan.
items.citation: Kajiwara N, Tsunetoshi Y, Shiode S. No detection of respiratory syncytial virus at one clinic in Japan with rapid immunochromatographic antigen tests for three viruses using the same nasopharyngeal swabs from adult patients. 2026

items.title: Can exercise affect immune function to increase susceptibility to infection?
items.summary: This debate article examined the longstanding question of whether exercise itself can suppress immune function and increase susceptibility to infection. The paper structured opposing arguments around four contested issues: whether athletes experience greater infection susceptibility than the general population, whether exercise independently alters immunity beyond confounding lifestyle factors, the validity of biomarkers used to assess immune health in those performing arduous exercise, and the overall quality of evidence supporting or refuting exercise-induced immune suppression. Moderate-intensity exercise of relatively short duration is broadly accepted as beneficial to immune defense, particularly in older adults and those with chronic disease, while high-performance athletes and military personnel show elevated infection burdens that have historically been attributed to strenuous training. However, the view that exercise per se drives this increased risk has been challenged, given that these populations simultaneously experience anxiety, sleep disruption, travel, nutritional deficits, and environmental extremes that activate overlapping immune pathways. Both sides agreed that infection susceptibility is multifactorial in origin, but whether exercise acts as an independent causative factor remains unresolved, prompting a call for more rigorous empirical research in exercise immunology.
items.citation: Richard J. Simpson, Richard J. Simpson, Maree Gleeson et al.. Can exercise affect immune function to increase susceptibility to infection?. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Spinal cord injury: Known and possible influences on the immune response to exercise
items.summary: This review paper examined how spinal cord injury affects immune function, with particular focus on the immune response to exercise. The authors conducted a comprehensive literature search across multiple databases to gather all available evidence on exercise immunology in individuals with spinal cord injury, spanning patient, recreationally active, and athlete populations. Spinal cord injury was found to compromise immunity through multiple pathways, including reduced lymphocyte numbers, autonomic dysfunction, and altered catecholamine concentrations, with these effects being especially pronounced in individuals with tetraplegia. However, certain immune responses to exercise, such as increases in natural killer cell cytotoxicity and mucosal immunity changes, appeared to occur independently of the catecholamine response or resembled those seen in able-bodied individuals, suggesting that compensatory mechanisms such as sympathetic reflex activity, receptor hypersensitivity, or neuroendocrine adjustments may partially offset injury-related immune deficits. The authors conclude that exercise and rehabilitation therapy show promise as tools to maintain or improve immune and autonomic function following spinal cord injury, while calling for further research to clarify the underlying mechanisms.
items.citation: Christof A. Leicht, Victoria L. Goosey‐Tolfrey, Nicolette C. Bishop. Spinal cord injury: Known and possible influences on the immune response to exercise. PubMed. 2026

items.title: The International Guideline for the Definition, Classification, Diagnosis and Management of Urticaria
items.summary: This paper presents an updated international clinical guideline for urticaria, a mast cell-driven condition characterized by wheals, angioedema, or both. The guideline was developed using Cochrane methodology and the GRADE framework, and was produced through a broad consensus process involving delegates from a large number of national and international societies across many countries. The document addresses the definition, classification, diagnosis, and management of urticaria, encompassing both acute and chronic forms, with chronic urticaria further subdivided into spontaneous and inducible subtypes. The guideline highlights that chronic urticaria is disabling and impairs quality of life, while also noting that novel therapeutic options are now available. The resulting recommendations are intended to provide expert-guided, evidence-based approaches to the full spectrum of urticaria subtypes.
items.citation: T. Zuberbier, Z. Abdul Hameed Ansari, A. H. Abdul Latiff et al.. The International Guideline for the Definition, Classification, Diagnosis and Management of Urticaria. Allergy. 2026

items.title: Tumour–brain crosstalk restrains cancer immunity via a sensory–sympathetic axis
items.summary: This paper investigated how tumors in peripheral organs communicate with the brain and how this crosstalk influences anti-tumor immunity. Using genetically engineered mouse models combined with neural tracing, tissue imaging, and single-cell transcriptomics in a lung adenocarcinoma model, the researchers mapped a bidirectional signaling axis between tumors and the central nervous system. They found that lung tumors activate vagal sensory neurons expressing a specific receptor, which transmit signals to brainstem nuclei and in turn drive increased sympathetic nervous system activity within the tumor microenvironment. This elevated sympathetic output suppresses anti-tumor immune responses by acting on alveolar macrophages through adrenergic signaling, thereby creating an immune-suppressive microenvironment that promotes tumor growth. Disrupting this sensory-to-sympathetic circuit through genetic, pharmacological, or chemogenetic means enhanced immune responses against the cancer and significantly reduced tumor growth, suggesting this tumor-brain axis as a potential therapeutic target.
items.citation: Haohan Karen Wei, Chuyue Yu, Bo Hu et al.. Tumour–brain crosstalk restrains cancer immunity via a sensory–sympathetic axis. Nature. 2026

items.title: Understanding graft-versus-host disease. Preliminary findings regarding the effects of exercise in affected patients
items.summary: This paper examines graft-versus-host disease, a serious immune-mediated complication arising when donor lymphocytes attack host tissues following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with particular focus on its chronic form and associated physical morbidity. The authors conducted a review of the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the disease alongside available evidence from both animal and human studies on the effects of exercise in affected patients. Their findings suggest that exercise training as an adjunct therapy holds promise for improving physical fitness, potentially enhancing immune function, and reducing fatigue in this population. However, the authors conclude that the existing evidence base is insufficient, calling for more randomized controlled trials that specifically target patients with graft-versus-host disease rather than broader transplant populations.
items.citation: Carmen Fiuza‐Luces, Nuria Garatachea, Nathan A. Berger et al.. Understanding graft-versus-host disease. Preliminary findings regarding the effects of exercise in affected patients. PubMed. 2026

items.title: Oncolytic viruses: advanced strategies in cancer therapy
items.summary: This review examines oncolytic viruses as a cancer immunotherapy strategy, focusing on their mechanisms of action, combination potential, and clinical translation challenges. Oncolytic viruses selectively infect and lyse tumor cells while inducing immunogenic cell death, promoting antigen presentation, and converting the tumor microenvironment from an immune-suppressive to an immune-permissive state. Beyond direct tumor killing, they modulate angiogenesis and extracellular matrix remodeling to disrupt tumor progression and metastasis. The review surveys how combining oncolytic viruses with chemotherapy, radiotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors, adoptive cell therapy, and epigenetic drugs produces synergistic antitumor effects and helps overcome treatment resistance. The authors also address persistent translational barriers—including viral dissemination, therapy resistance, and regulatory complexity—and propose future directions for optimizing oncolytic virus therapy in clinical practice.
items.citation: Danli Xiao, Huarong Zhang, Ye Liu et al.. Oncolytic viruses: advanced strategies in cancer therapy. Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. 2026

items.title: Emulating the nonlinear effects of modified gravity on the matter power spectrum for reconstruction
items.summary: This paper addresses the computational bottleneck of incorporating nonlinear modified gravity effects into model-independent reconstructions of modified gravity functions, where repeated evaluations of the nonlinear matter power spectrum are prohibitively expensive. The authors built a neural-network emulator trained on nearly a million samples to predict the nonlinear correction ratio of the modified gravity nonlinear power spectrum to its linear counterpart, using the CosmoPower framework. The emulator achieves sub-percent to low-percent level accuracy across a wide range of scales and cosmological parameters, recovering standard cosmological and general relativity limits in synthetic data tests, demonstrating its reliability for Stage-IV-like surveys. Beyond serving as a fast surrogate for likelihood evaluations, the emulator is shown to break degeneracies between models with nearly identical linear power spectra, to interface with current photometric survey likelihoods, and to enable forecasting of future combined survey constraints via principal component analysis. The work thus provides both a practical tool and a validation framework for efficient nonlinear modified gravity analyses.
items.citation: Lanyang Yi, Kazuya Koyama, Qi Xiong et al.. Emulating the nonlinear effects of modified gravity on the matter power spectrum for reconstruction. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Dark Photons from Perturbative Decay of a Misaligned Higgs Field
items.summary: This paper investigates the production of dark photons as a dark matter candidate through the perturbative decay of a dark Higgs field that is displaced from its potential minimum during inflation, a process known as stochastic misalignment. The framework provides a predictive mechanism for generating the dark photon relic abundance, with constraints arising from structure formation due to the initially boosted nature of the produced dark photons, and from inflationary isocurvature fluctuations that require small quartic couplings. The study identifies viable dark photon masses and gauge couplings consistent with this scenario, finding that the allowed parameter space becomes more tightly constrained when kinetic mixing between the dark photon and the Standard Model photon is present. The authors suggest the favored parameter regions could be tested by future cosmic microwave background or Lyman-alpha observations, and through direct detection experiments or diffuse soft gamma-ray searches if kinetic mixing is present.
items.citation: James M. Cline, Gonzalo Herrera, Jean-Samuel Roux. Dark Photons from Perturbative Decay of a Misaligned Higgs Field. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Spectrum Estimation is Almost as Hard as Tomography
items.summary: This paper investigates how many copies of an unknown quantum state are required to estimate or test its fundamental unitarily invariant properties, specifically spectrum estimation, von Neumann entropy estimation, and rank-testing. The authors establish sample complexity lower bounds for all three tasks in terms of the dimension of the quantum state, showing that the required number of samples scales nearly quadratically with dimension. To prove these lower bounds, they construct hard instances using sandwiched products of Haar-random projectors and develop a novel normalization technique that yields explicit expressions for high-order tensor moments, which are analyzed through symmetric functions of Jucys–Murphy elements in the symmetric group algebra. Indistinguishability of the constructed hard instances is demonstrated by analyzing log-likelihood ratios, performing moment-matching to eliminate low-order components, and bounding an f-divergence through high-order terms. These results imply that estimating even basic spectral properties of quantum states is nearly as sample-intensive as full quantum state tomography, significantly tightening our understanding of the classical shadow and related quantum property testing problems.
items.citation: Marco Fanizza, Ryan O'Donnell, Chirag Wadhwa. Spectrum Estimation is Almost as Hard as Tomography. arXiv. 2026

items.title: ArcLP: A Matlab implementation of an $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n}L)$ arc-search infeasible interior-point algorithm for linear programming
items.summary: This paper presents a Matlab software implementation of an arc-search infeasible interior-point algorithm for linear programming that carries the best known polynomial complexity bound among interior-point methods for this class of problems. The authors describe the software architecture, key algorithmic strategies, and ease of use, illustrating the implementation with a worked example. The code was extensively tested on standard Netlib benchmark linear programming problems spanning a wide range of problem sizes, including instances with tens of thousands of constraints and hundreds of thousands of variables, and it successfully found optimal solutions in all cases. Computational results were compared against the widely used Mehrotra predictor-corrector algorithm, and the arc-search implementation was found to be competitive in practice while also possessing superior theoretical complexity guarantees.
items.citation: Yang, Yaguang. ArcLP: A Matlab implementation of an $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{n}L)$ arc-search infeasible interior-point algorithm for linear programming. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Fermionic entropy: an efficiently measurable strong monotone for non-Gaussianity
items.summary: This paper investigates fermionic non-Gaussianity as a quantum resource, focusing on how to rigorously quantify and experimentally measure deviations from the classically tractable class of fermionic Gaussian states. The authors introduce the fermionic entropy, defined via the squared Frobenius norm of the correlation matrix, and prove it constitutes a strong monotone under Gaussian operations for pure states, with an associated fermionic purity that can be estimated from a number of two-copy measurements independent of system size. They establish that fermionic entropy satisfies asymptotic continuity, which yields an operational interpretation as an upper bound on the asymptotic rate of non-Gaussianity distillation, and they derive an improved sample complexity bound for tolerant testing of fermionic Gaussian states. As a further application, they analyze Matchgate circuits supplemented with Majorana-local non-Gaussian gates and prove that a linear number of such gates is necessary to approximate a state two-design below a small error threshold, matching known upper bounds up to logarithmic factors and thereby determining the optimal doping level for generating Haar-like quantum dynamics in this architecture.
items.citation: Lorenzo Leone, Lennart Bittel. Fermionic entropy: an efficiently measurable strong monotone for non-Gaussianity. arXiv. 2026

items.title: The IACOB project XIX. Revisiting massive-star evolution with empirical TAMS constraints: updated models, overshoot calibration, and the population of blue supergiants
items.summary: This paper investigates the physical processes governing massive-star evolution, focusing on convective boundary mixing and the role of binary interactions in shaping observed stellar populations. The authors used empirical observations of massive Galactic stars from the IACOB database, specifically the recently established location of the Terminal Age Main Sequence, to calibrate convective boundary mixing efficiency in single-star evolutionary models. Multiple grids of stellar evolution models were computed with varying overshoot calibrations, angular momentum transport prescriptions, initial masses, and rotation rates, and synthetic populations were generated for direct comparison with observations. The calibrated models successfully reproduce the empirical main-sequence width for slowly rotating stars when a mass-dependent overshooting efficiency is adopted, and rotational properties of observed populations are well reproduced by single-star models regardless of angular momentum transport assumptions. However, single-star models fail to explain the velocity dependence of the terminal-age main-sequence location and cannot account for the observed population of blue supergiants beyond the main sequence, suggesting that binary interactions are necessary to explain these features.
items.citation: Luca Sciarini, Abel de Burgos, Sophie Rosu et al.. The IACOB project XIX. Revisiting massive-star evolution with empirical TAMS constraints: updated models, overshoot calibration, and the population of blue supergiants. arXiv. 2026

items.title: Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.
items.summary: This paper reviews advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarker research over roughly a five-year period, synthesizing the scientific evidence that has informed updated WHO policy guidance consolidating recommendations for tuberculosis detection and drug-resistance testing into a single framework. Key diagnostic developments include the expanded role of digital chest radiography with computer-aided detection as a screening and triage tool, and the broadened deployment of decentralized molecular platforms such as low-complexity automated and manual nucleic acid amplification tests across diverse specimen types including stool, gastric aspirate, nasopharyngeal samples, and tongue swabs, which has particularly improved bacteriological confirmation in children. Rapid molecular drug-resistance testing has progressed, and targeted next-generation sequencing is now WHO-endorsed for comprehensive drug-susceptibility testing at reference laboratory level, while urine lipoarabinomannan assays offer diagnostic benefit in people with HIV and advanced disease but remain limited in broader application. In the biomarker space, host blood transcriptomic signatures demonstrate promising prognostic and triage performance, and proteomic, metabolomic, cellular, and pathogen-derived markers are under clinical evaluation, yet none has met WHO target product profile criteria for a point-of-care test capable of reliably distinguishing infection from disease, including subclinical tuberculosis. The paper identifies persistent performance, implementation, and equity gaps as priorities requiring further development.
items.citation: Walzl G, McHugh TD, Chakaya J et al.. Advances in tuberculosis diagnostics and biomarkers, 2020-26: scientific evidence, recommendations, gaps, and developmental priorities.. The Lancet. Microbe. 2027

items.title: AI-Enhanced Point-of-Care Diagnostics for Infectious Diseases in Resource-Limited Settings: A Scoping Review.
items.summary: This scoping review systematically mapped research on artificial intelligence-enhanced point-of-care and rapid diagnostic technologies for infectious diseases in resource-limited settings, examining disease coverage, geographic representation, and the rigor of study validation. Following established scoping review methodology, the authors searched five major databases spanning over a decade of literature, screening more than a thousand records and ultimately including over two hundred studies. The field was found to be growing exponentially, though research was heavily concentrated on a narrow set of diseases—COVID-19, malaria, and tuberculosis—while neglected tropical diseases were markedly underrepresented, and convolutional neural networks were the dominant artificial intelligence approach across diagnostic modalities. Geographic coverage was skewed toward East Africa and South Asia, leaving West Africa and Latin America underserved in the literature. A critical finding was that the vast majority of studies lacked prospective field validation, revealing a substantial gap between laboratory-stage development and real-world deployment readiness, which the authors argue must be addressed alongside greater disease equity and meaningful community involvement in future research.
items.venue: Tropical medicine & international health : TM & IH
items.citation: Farquhar H. AI-Enhanced Point-of-Care Diagnostics for Infectious Diseases in Resource-Limited Settings: A Scoping Review.. Tropical medicine & international health : TM & IH. 2026

items.title: Point-of-care testing (POCT) for Infectious diseases: technological innovation, effectiveness evaluation, and application strategies in resource-limited regions.
items.summary: This paper presents a systematic review of point-of-care testing technologies applied to infectious disease diagnosis, with a particular focus on their role in early screening, epidemic surveillance, and public health prevention. The review covers recent technological innovations across molecular diagnostics, microfluidic systems, biosensing platforms, and artificial intelligence integration. It also examines the quality assessment frameworks used to evaluate these technologies, addressing performance indicators such as sensitivity, specificity, detection limits, stability, and suitability for field deployment. Particular emphasis is placed on strategies for implementing point-of-care testing in resource-limited settings, including approaches to optimizing technical applicability, resource allocation, and local support infrastructure. The paper concludes by identifying current challenges and proposing future development directions, intending to provide both theoretical and practical guidance for advancing infectious disease diagnostics in underserved contexts.
items.citation: Zhang YX, Ru JF. Point-of-care testing (POCT) for Infectious diseases: technological innovation, effectiveness evaluation, and application strategies in resource-limited regions.. Diagnostic microbiology and infectious disease. 2026
